# scenario: interface-claimed-elsewhere
# inventory: one-built-in-radio
# usable: true
# blast radius: network

## bindings
- uplink:wan-eth: bound → end0

## findings
- (none)

## notes
- This profile hosts no access point. That is a valid state — a device with no radio, or one reached over Ethernet only — but nothing will serve the local network.

## sysctl
- net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=2 — a tunnel bound to its own interface would otherwise have its replies discarded by the kernel
- net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter=2 — so an interface a tunnel creates later inherits the same setting

## units
- wf-firewall.service enabled=true active=true — loads the generated firewall ruleset
- wf-firewall-ready.target enabled=true active=true — ordering marker: the generated ruleset is loaded
- wf-rederive.service enabled=true active=false — re-derives the environment-dependent configuration before the core reads it
- wf-route-check.service enabled=true active=false — checks that the device can still reach the networks it is on, once the tunnel exists
- wf-hostapd@.service enabled=false active=false — access point template; the instance is the interface name
- wf-supplicant@.service enabled=false active=false — wireless client template; the instance is the interface name
- wf-dhcp@.service enabled=false active=false — address server template; the instance is the interface name
- wf-openvpn@.service enabled=false active=false — external tunnel daemon template; the instance is the tunnel id
- wf-transport@.service enabled=false active=false — obfuscation transport template; the instance is the transport id
- wf-socks@.service enabled=false active=false — external client template; the instance is the tunnel id
- wf-core.service enabled=true active=true — the proxy core: the data plane

## plan, in apply order
- WARNING: this change reconfigures end0, which is carrying the connection you are using right now. You will probably lose access while it applies. Make sure you have a second way in — another network, or a cable — before confirming, because the confirmation has to come from you and the device reverts on its own if it does not arrive.
- write /etc/sysctl.d/90-wayfarer.conf — makes the kernel settings survive a reboot
- write /etc/wayfarer/core/config.json — the proxy core configuration
- write /etc/wayfarer/fence.json — which networks in the core exclusion list are followed tunnel networks
- write /etc/wayfarer/nftables.conf — the firewall ruleset
- write /etc/wayfarer/README — says what owns this directory
- write /usr/local/lib/systemd/system/wf-firewall.service — the unit definition for wf-firewall.service

## generated files

### /etc/sysctl.d/90-wayfarer.conf (mode 644)
purpose: makes the kernel settings survive a reboot
```
# Generated by Wayfarer from the profile "Contested".
# Edits here are overwritten on the next apply. Change the profile instead.
#
# These are applied live on every apply as well. This file is what makes them survive a
# reboot, which the running kernel does not.

# a tunnel bound to its own interface would otherwise have its replies discarded by the kernel
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 2

# so an interface a tunnel creates later inherits the same setting
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 2
```

### /etc/systemd/network/20-wayfarer-wan-eth.network (mode 644)
purpose: addressing for uplink "wan-eth" on end0
```
# Generated by Wayfarer from the profile "Contested".
# Edits here are overwritten on the next apply. Change the profile instead.

[Match]
Name=end0

[Network]
DHCP=ipv4

# IPv6 is not accepted on the uplink either. A router advertisement here would give the
# device a routable v6 address and a default route, and traffic would leave outside the
# tunnel — which is the leak the access-point side is already rejecting.
IPv6AcceptRA=no

[DHCPv4]
# Routes come from the uplink, but the resolver does not: the core is the resolver, and
# a pushed one written into the host configuration is a second answer nobody asked for.
UseDNS=no
UseDomains=no
RouteMetric=110

[Link]
# An uplink that is not present must not hold up boot. A device with no uplink is a valid,
# expected state, and waiting for one would delay the access point that makes the device
# reachable in the first place.
RequiredForOnline=no
```

### /etc/wayfarer/nftables.conf (mode 600)
purpose: the firewall ruleset
```
# Generated by Wayfarer from the profile "Contested".
# Edits here are overwritten on the next apply. Change the profile instead.

#
# Only the table below is touched. Tables belonging to other software on this device —
# including the one a proxy core creates for redirection — are left exactly as they are.

table inet wayfarer {}
delete table inet wayfarer

table inet wayfarer {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority filter; policy accept;
    ct state established,related accept
    iif lo accept


    # Reachable from the network this device is a CLIENT of, because the profile asks for
    # it (services.management.onUplinkNetwork). What that exposes and to whom is stated
    # where the choice is made; behind it stand password authentication, a lockout
    # counted in uptime rather than wall-clock time, and an API that is off until a
    # human turns it on.
    iifname "end0" tcp dport 8088 accept

    # A tunnel is never a management surface. Not a setting, and deliberately not one.
    iifname "tun*" tcp dport 8088 reject with tcp reset
    iifname "wg*" tcp dport 8088 reject with tcp reset
  }

  chain forward {
    type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept;

    # Clamp the segment size to the path MTU. A tunnel lowers the effective MTU and the
    # symptom of not clamping is that small requests work and large ones hang, which is
    # diagnosed as "the internet is slow" rather than as a configuration fault.
    tcp flags syn tcp option maxseg size set rt mtu

    # See the input chain: rejected, not dropped, and at the access point.
    meta nfproto ipv6 reject with icmpv6 admin-prohibited

    # The kill-switch is off. With no tunnel configured yet, a kill-switch on makes a
    # working device look broken, so it is a switch rather than a policy baked in.

  }

  chain output {
    type route hook output priority mangle; policy accept;

    # Time synchronisation is labelled by DESTINATION PORT and not by user, and the policy
    # rule that acts on it is installed by the firewall unit using the same ports.
    # By port because the time service does not run as root, so a rule written in
    # terms of the root user misses it entirely — and this failure is self-locking:
    # correcting a wrong clock needs a time query, and transports that authenticate on a
    # timestamp refuse to connect while the clock is wrong. Every tunnel then looks
    # broken while every direct connection works.
    udp dport { 123 } meta mark set 0x1e7
    tcp dport { 123 } meta mark set 0x1e7

    # A label on the device's own traffic. **It does not route anything by itself, and the
    # routing is not done here.** Keeping the tunnel off this traffic is the job of the policy
    # rules the firewall unit installs, which select on user and destination port.
    #
    # That split is a measurement, not a preference. A policy rule matching this mark was tried
    # and broke the device's own networking outright: the source address is chosen on the FIRST
    # route lookup, before this chain runs and therefore before the mark exists, so the packet
    # already carried the tunnel's own address — and the reroute a mark triggers keeps a source
    # that is still local. Packets left the physical interface with an address the upstream
    # cannot reply to. A mark cannot fix a source that has already been chosen.
    #
    # It is kept because it is a true statement about the packet that costs nothing, and the
    # proxy core is free to use it. Nothing in this project routes on it.
    meta skuid 0 meta mark set 0x1e7
  }

  chain postrouting {
    type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept;
    oifname "end0" masquerade
  }
}
```

purpose: says what owns this directory

# Generated by Wayfarer from the profile "Contested".
# Edits here are overwritten on the next apply. Change the profile instead.
#
# Everything under this directory is generated from the active profile and is replaced on every
# apply. Editing a file here has no lasting effect: change the profile instead.

# device did not generate are never started, stopped or removed by it.

### /usr/local/lib/systemd/system/wf-core.service (mode 644)
purpose: the unit definition for wf-core.service
```
# Generated by Wayfarer. Edits here are overwritten on the next apply.
#
# Runs the proxy core against the generated configuration, and nothing else.
#
# This unit is owned exclusively by Wayfarer: nothing else on this device installs, starts or
# stops it, and Wayfarer does the same for units it did not generate.

[Unit]
Description=Wayfarer proxy core
Requires=wf-firewall-ready.target
Requires=wf-rederive.service
After=network.target wf-firewall-ready.target wf-rederive.service
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sing-box run -c /etc/wayfarer/core/config.json -D /var/lib/wayfarer/core
ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/sing-box check -c /etc/wayfarer/core/config.json
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3
LimitNOFILE=65536
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_ADMIN CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_ADMIN CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/wayfarer
ProtectHome=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

### /usr/local/lib/systemd/system/wf-firewall.service (mode 644)
purpose: the unit definition for wf-firewall.service
```
# Generated by Wayfarer. Edits here are overwritten on the next apply.
#
# Loads the generated nftables ruleset. Our table only; nothing else is flushed.
#
# This unit is owned exclusively by Wayfarer: nothing else on this device installs, starts or
# stops it, and Wayfarer does the same for units it did not generate.

[Unit]
Description=Wayfarer firewall ruleset
DefaultDependencies=no
After=sysinit.target
Before=network-pre.target
Wants=network-pre.target
Conflicts=shutdown.target
Before=shutdown.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=yes
ExecStartPre=/usr/sbin/nft -c -f /etc/wayfarer/nftables.conf
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/nft -f /etc/wayfarer/nftables.conf
ExecStartPost=/bin/sh -c 'while /usr/sbin/ip rule del priority 8000 2>/dev/null; do :; done; /usr/sbin/ip rule add priority 8000 uidrange 0-0 iif lo lookup main'
ExecStartPost=/bin/sh -c 'while /usr/sbin/ip rule del priority 8001 2>/dev/null; do :; done; /usr/sbin/ip rule add priority 8001 ipproto udp dport 123 iif lo lookup main'
ExecStartPost=/bin/sh -c 'while /usr/sbin/ip rule del priority 8002 2>/dev/null; do :; done; /usr/sbin/ip rule add priority 8002 ipproto tcp dport 123 iif lo lookup main'
# No ExecStop: see the generator comment. Stopping this unit must not remove the rules, and
# nothing here may flush a ruleset that other software has tables in.

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```
